## Why Identifying Top Talent Has Become More Difficult


**Finding top talent** has always required **good judgment** , but the landscape has shifted. The familiar signs recruiters once relied on now create more[noise than signal](https://philarchive.org/rec/MALEDT) , making it harder to identify **the candidates who truly matter** .


> "The familiar signs recruiters once relied on now create more **noise than signal** , drowning out the talent organizations need most."


⚠️ **Warning:** Relying on **traditional hiring signals** in today's market is no longer reliable. The landscape has *fundamentally* shifted.


According to the[SocialTalent 2025 Hiring Reality Check](https://www.socialtalent.com/leadership/the-2025-hiring-reality-check-data-driven-answers-to-ta-leaders-top-questions) , **applications per role** have increased by ***up to 300%*** in *some* industries. **More applications** don't mean **more qualified candidates** — they mean *more time* separating **relevant information** from **irrelevant volume** , and **greater risk** that **strong candidates** get lost before their resume is *properly* reviewed.


## What's Increased


- Applications per role (up to 300%)
More time spent filtering, less time evaluating


- Volume of unqualified submissions
Higher risk of missing top candidates


- Recruiter workload
Greater chance of strong talent being overlooked


🔑 **Takeaway:** A ***300% surge*** in applications doesn't create **more opportunity** — it creates **more noise** , and *that* noise is costing organizations their **best hires** .


💡 **Key Point:** The **real challenge** isn't attracting applicants — it's building a process that ensures **top talent** isn't buried under *irrelevant volume* before they ever get a fair look.


### Why volume alone does not solve the quality problem


The failure point is usually not a shortage of applicants, but a shortage of the right signals within that pool. A recruiter reviewing 400 CVs for a single role is not four times more likely to find the right person than one reviewing 100; they are simply four times more likely to miss something important or default to the most familiar-looking profile. When 63% of employers identify skills gaps as a major barrier to business transformation, according to the[World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025](https://www.weforum.org/publications/the-future-of-jobs-report-2025/digest/) , the candidates who look most qualified on paper are not always the ones best equipped to close those gaps.


#### Why do fixed filters miss the candidates who matter most?


Most teams reduce applicants using fixed filters: job titles, years of experience, and educational background. This approach is fast and requires no additional tools, but it systematically excludes candidates who developed relevant skills through non-linear paths, adjacent roles, or unconventional experience. When hiring workflows fragment across spreadsheets, email threads, and disconnected tools, those candidates never surface. A[global HR system](https://www.cercli.com/) like Cercli that brings candidate scoring and screening into the same environment as your other hiring data surfaces what matters before manual review.


### What experience actually tells you


Two candidates with the same years of experience can have markedly different skill levels, adaptability, and practical judgment. Experience indicates someone has worked in a role—not what they accomplished, how they handled stress, or whether they learned and improved. According to the[SocialTalent 2025 Hiring Reality Check](https://www.socialtalent.com/leadership/the-2025-hiring-reality-check-data-driven-answers-to-ta-leaders-top-questions) , only 1 in 4 talent acquisition leaders feel confident assessing candidate quality at scale, suggesting the problem lies not in volume but in the criteria used.


#### Why does experience mislead when hiring across borders?


The same challenge applies when hiring across borders. Job titles carry different weight in different markets, and educational credentials vary by country. A candidate from one country may present their experience in unfamiliar ways to a recruiter trained on local customs, even when their underlying capability is strong. Without a consistent framework for evaluating what candidates can do rather than where they have done it,[international hiring](https://www.cercli.com/resources/ai-in-recruitment-examples) rewards familiarity over fit.


#### What should hiring processes measure instead?


The harder question is what you should examine instead and why so many[hiring processes](https://www.cercli.com/resources/applicant-tracking-system-functional-requirements) still rely on misleading indicators.

## Why Traditional Approaches to Identifying Top Talent Can Fall Short


**Traditional hiring signals mislead** more often than *most teams admit* . The **perfect resume** , **brilliant interview performance** , and **prestigious employer name** create *false certainty* — painting a picture that looks compelling on paper but *rarely* reflects **real-world performance** .


> " **74% of employers** admit they've hired the wrong person for a position — suggesting the problem is *structural* , not isolated." —[salesassessmenttesting.com](https://salesassessmenttesting.com/blog/why-traditional-hiring-methods-fall-short/)


### Traditional Signal


- Perfect Resume


- Why It Falls Short: Reflects presentation skills, not job performance


- Brilliant Interview


- Why It Falls Short: Rewards rehearsed answers, not real capability


- Prestigious Employer Name


- Why It Falls Short: Signals past environment, not transferable talent


🚨 **Warning:** Relying on *surface-level* hiring signals doesn't filter for **top talent** — it filters for **top performers at interviewing** . These are *not* the same thing.


🔑 **Takeaway:** When ***74% of employers*** confess to a **bad hire** , this isn't a streak of bad luck — it's a **structural flaw** baked into *traditional* hiring methods. The signals teams trust most are *often* the ones that mislead them most.


### Why do familiar hiring signals break down?


The failure point is usually invisible until after the hire. Years of experience indicate how long someone has held a role, not how much they've grown within it. A polished interview shows how well[someone performs under social pressure](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0148296319301985) , not how they'll handle confusion when a project changes direction. These proxies feel like evidence because they're measurable, but they measure the wrong things. Capability isn't the same as credentials, and potential rarely announces itself through a keyword match.


#### How do disconnected workflows make blind spots worse?


Disconnected hiring workflows reinforce these blind spots. When candidate information lives across multiple tools and spreadsheets, decision-making defaults to the easiest signal to retrieve—usually the most superficial one.[Cercli addresses this](https://www.cercli.com/) by consolidating hiring, HR, and workforce management into a single platform, surfacing the signals that matter to decision-makers without manual assembly.


### Why attitude outlasts ability on paper


[LinkedIn Pulse's 2025 Talent Acquisition Trend report](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/2025-talent-acquisition-trend-every-ta-leader-needs-know-4geee) found that only 11% of new hires fail because they lack technical skills, while[89% fail because of attitude, motivation](https://icma.org/sites/default/files/6135_.pdf) , or temperament. Yet most screening processes focus on evaluating the 11% factor through technical tests and qualification boxes, while treating motivation and cultural alignment as something to gauge in a 30-minute conversation. The imbalance reflects what's easiest to measure, not what's most predictive.


### The bias toward the familiar


The same issue shows up in talent assessment and product design: familiarity looks like quality. Hiring teams are drawn to candidates who resemble top performers already in-house—same career path, industry background, communication style. This looks like pattern recognition but is closer to confirmation bias. Cultural fit, when properly defined, means working effectively within a team's values and environment, not reminding decision-makers of someone they already trust. When fit gets confused with familiarity, strong candidates from unconventional paths get filtered out before evaluation.


The frustrating part is that this isn't even the hardest piece to solve.


## The Biggest Challenges When Identifying Top Talent


Finding[top talent](https://www.cercli.com/resources/ai-candidate-screening) involves **many challenges** that *build on each other* , often in places you **don't expect** .


> "Identifying top talent is rarely a single obstacle — it's a **cascade of compounding challenges** that can derail even the most experienced hiring teams." — Talent Acquisition Research


🎯 **Key Point:** **Top talent identification** is *not* a linear process — every stage introduces **new complexity** , from **sourcing** and **screening** to **bias** and **decision fatigue** .


⚠️ **Warning:** Underestimating how these challenges **compound over time** is one of the *most common* mistakes hiring teams make — leading to **missed candidates** , **longer time-to-hire** , and **costly mis-hires** .


### Challenge Area


- **Sourcing the right candidates**


- Limits your talent pool from the start


- **Screening at scale**


- Increases time-to-hire and decision fatigue


- **Unconscious bias**


- Skews evaluation accuracy


- **Predicting cultural fit**


- Leads to costly mis-hires


### When confidence is the first casualty


Most hiring teams work with less certainty than they admit. According to the[SHRM State of Recruiting 2025 Benchmarking Report](https://www.shrm.org/executive-network/insights/people-strategy/state-of-recruiting-2025-insights-to-maximize-recruitment) , only 1 in 4 HR professionals report confidence in their ability to identify top talent. This means most people responsible for talent decisions operate with significant doubt, often lacking the structured criteria or consolidated data needed to reduce it.


### Why does fragmentation cause hiring decisions to break down?


The failure point is usually fragmentation. A candidate's resume sits in one system, interview notes live in a shared document that nobody updates consistently, assessment results are in a separate tool, and the hiring manager's impressions exist only in memory or email. When candidate information scatters across disconnected workflows, hiring teams cannot build a complete picture of who they are evaluating. Decisions get made on whichever fragments are easiest to access, not on the full picture.


#### How does manual coordination create gaps as candidate volumes grow?


Most teams rely on whoever can pull information together fastest, usually a recruiter juggling too many roles. As candidate volumes grow and roles become more complex, manual coordination creates gaps: strong candidates get delayed, comparisons become inconsistent, and the reasoning behind past hiring decisions becomes impossible to reconstruct. Our[global HR system](https://www.cercli.com/) brings together hiring, HR, and workforce data in one place, enabling teams to evaluate candidates against consistent criteria rather than piecing together information from scattered sources.


### The measurement problem nobody solves early enough


[Lloyd Staffing's research](https://www.lloydstaffing.com/hiring-challenges/) on the biggest hiring challenges of 2025 shows that a bad hire can cost up to 30% of that employee's first-year earnings. Most organizations fail to connect their hiring process to post-hire outcomes. They track candidate progression through interviews but not which early signs predicted strong performance, employee retention, or time to productivity. Without this feedback loop, hiring teams repeat the same evaluation patterns without knowing which ones work.


### Why is assessing future potential so difficult?


Predicting what someone will do in the future is harder than assessing what they have done in the past. Most hiring processes are not designed for this. The ability to learn quickly, adapt to change, and solve problems under stress separates candidates who will grow in their roles from those who will plateau. These traits rarely appear on a resume and are difficult to measure in a single interview. Using consistent evaluation standards for all candidates gives hiring teams a better way to compare qualities they cannot directly observe.


#### What happens when strong candidates are kept waiting?


Strong candidates rarely wait. They explore multiple job opportunities simultaneously, and delays in[screening or feedback](https://www.cercli.com/resources/automated-candidate-screening) give competitors the advantage. Knowing which signals matter and acting quickly separates effective processes from those that lose top talent before the offer stage.


That gap between knowing what to look for and finding it faster is where things get interesting.


## 10 Practical Ways to Identify Top Talent


**Identifying**[top talent](https://www.cercli.com/resources/ats-features) is a series of **careful decisions** , each one *filtering for what matters* over what doesn't — until the **right person** becomes *clear* rather than debatable.


> "The difference between a **great hire** and a costly mistake often comes down to whether the process was *intentional* — or improvised." — Hiring Best Practices


💡 **Tip:** Treat every stage of your **talent identification process** as a *deliberate filter* , not a formality. Each step should eliminate noise and surface **genuine signal** .


### Stage


- **Job Definition**


- **What You're Filtering For:** Must-have skills & behaviors
- **Common Mistake:** Vague or inflated requirements


- **CV Review**


- **What You're Filtering For:** Evidence of performance
- **Common Mistake:** Judging on presentation alone


- **Screening Call**


- **What You're Filtering For:** Communication & motivation
- **Common Mistake:** Skipping this step entirely


- **Structured Interview**


- **What You're Filtering For:** Role-specific competencies
- **Common Mistake:** Unstructured, gut-feel questions


- **Reference Check**


- **What You're Filtering For:** Behavioral confirmation
- **Common Mistake:** Treating it as a rubber stamp


🎯 **Key Point:** **Top talent identification** isn't a single decision — it's a *system* of compounding filters that makes the **right hire** undeniable.


**Define what success looks like** before the[first CV arrives](https://www.cercli.com/resources/applicant-tracking-system-benefits) . Without **specific, measurable criteria** , every candidate gets measured against a *different invisible standard* , where **good candidates get lost,** and weaker ones slip through. Write down the role's **must-have skills** , **performance-linked behaviors** , and what the **first six to twelve months** should produce. This definition becomes your **filter** , *not* your gut feeling.


⚠️ **Warning:** Skipping the **upfront success definition** is one of the *most common* and costly hiring mistakes. Without it, your process measures *impressions* , not **potential** .


✅ **Best Practice:** Before opening any role, document **three things** : the *non-negotiable* skills, the **key behaviors** tied to performance, and the **measurable outcomes** expected within the first **6–12 months** .


### 1. Define success before you screen for it


The most common[hiring mistake](https://www.cercli.com/resources/best-applicant-tracking-systems-for-small-businesses) occurs when a recruiter and hiring manager disagree on what they're seeking. Vague requirements default to familiarity: the candidate who resembles the previous hire or boasts the most recognizable employer. Neither reliably predicts performance.


Separate requirements into three categories: non-negotiable skills, desirable experience, and behaviors that correlate with strong performance in this environment. Agree on what good output looks like at six months. This shared standard makes every subsequent decision faster and more defensible.


### 2. Look past the title, into the work


Job titles are organizational labels, not capability certificates. A "Senior Coordinator" at one company may carry more relevant responsibility than a "Manager" at another. Title screening follows convention, not capability.


Build a skills profile instead. Identify the core technical and functional capabilities the role requires, then look for evidence of those capabilities regardless of title. This expands your talent pool considerably, particularly when hiring from adjacent industries or international markets where title conventions differ.


### 3. What someone achieved matters more than what they were assigned


Responsibilities describe a job. Achievements describe a person. A CV listing "managed client relationships" tells you almost nothing. A candidate who explains how they retained a key account during a contract dispute and its outcome tells you much more.


When reviewing applications, push for specifics: what was the situation, what did you do, and what changed as a result? Measurable outcomes—revenue, retention, cost reduction, or process improvement—are far more predictive than a list of duties. The candidate who answers clearly has already demonstrated a critical skill: connecting effort to results.


### 4. Transferable skills are undervalued, consistently


The failure point is a narrow definition of relevant experience. Teams reject candidates from adjacent industries because their background doesn't match exactly, even when their underlying capabilities align with the role's needs. Project management, analytical thinking, stakeholder communication, and problem-solving transfer across sectors.


When your talent pool is limited, identify the core capabilities the role demands and look for evidence of those capabilities in whatever context the candidate developed them. The candidate who built client management skills in logistics may outperform one from a more familiar sector because they have[already demonstrated adaptability](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0191308524000017) .


### 5. Skills assessments close the gap between claim and proof


A CV is a candidate's best argument for themselves. Skills assessments test whether that argument holds up. Work samples, technical exercises, case studies, and job simulations let candidates demonstrate what they can do rather than simply describe it.


Keep assessments short and focused on the specific role: a writing exercise for content roles, a data task for analysts, or a case study for consulting hires. The goal is to create evidence, not barriers. Candidates who perform well on realistic tasks are far more likely to perform well in the role itself, a connection stronger than any interview impression.


### 6. Structured interviews reduce the influence of first impressions


Unstructured interviews reward interview comfort over job-related skills. When interviewers ask different questions to different candidates and score based on overall impression, the process becomes a[comparison of feelings](https://www.testpartnership.com/blog/structured-vs-unstructured-interviews.html) rather than evidence.


Structured interviews fix this by using consistent behavioral and[situational questions](https://www.indeed.com/career-advice/interviewing/situational-interview-questions-and-answers) tied to skills that matter for the role. Build a scorecard with clear criteria before conversations start, then compare scores across candidates using the same framework. This approach improves fairness and makes decisions easier to justify.


### 7. Potential is a signal, not a consolation prize


Experience shows what someone has done. Potential shows what they can do next. For fast-growing companies or roles with evolving responsibilities,[potential is often more important](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9200749/) .


Look for learning agility: how quickly has this person learned new skills? Find examples of unfamiliar challenges they completed successfully. Look for curiosity shown through questions rather than answers. A candidate who has consistently grown into bigger responsibilities demonstrates more strength than one who has held the same job for a decade.


### 8. Use AI to surface what manual screening misses


Most teams manage early screening manually: a recruiter reviews applications one by one, applies a rough mental filter, and flags relevant ones. This process is slow, inconsistent, and prone to bias. When application volumes are high, candidates who arrived first get reviewed, not the most qualified.


#### How does AI screening identify stronger candidates faster?


AI-assisted screening processes large groups of job candidates, identifies relevant skills across backgrounds, and finds candidates who match job requirements regardless of how they describe their experience.[According to 80Twenty](https://www.80twenty.com/how-to-attract-top-talent/) , top talent is usually off the market within 10 days; moving fast to find and engage strong candidates is a competitive advantage. AI removes the bottleneck preventing recruiters from exercising judgment on the right people.


#### What happens when screening tools don't connect to the rest of your workflow?


Most teams using AI for screening rely on separate tools for sourcing, assessment, and candidate management, creating friction between steps.[Platforms like Cercli](https://www.cercli.com/) bring AI-native candidate scoring and HR workflows into a single system, so candidates identified through intelligent screening move directly to decision-makers without data loss between tools.


### 9. Your existing talent pool is an underused asset


Every organization has a backlog of strong candidates who weren't hired due to timing, competition, or role changes, yet most are never contacted again. This represents significant waste.


Maintain searchable talent pools of previous applicants, referrals, and interested candidates. When a new role opens, search that pool before launching a new campaign. Candidates who already understand your organization and have been assessed can move through the process faster with greater confidence on both sides. According to[Universum Global's 2025 research on attracting top talent](https://universumglobal.com/resources/blog/attracting-top-talent/) , top talent can be up to 8x more productive than average employees, meaning re-engaging one strong candidate from your existing pool can have an outsized impact on team performance.


### 10. Why is no single assessment method enough?


Every assessment method has a blind spot. A CV shows history but not adaptability. An interview reveals communication skills but not work execution. A work sample tests output but not collaboration. References provide background but don't predict future performance. The strongest hiring decisions combine multiple signals rather than relying on a single one.


#### What does a practical multi-method hiring process look like?


A practical process for a mid-to-senior hire might include a skills and experience review, an achievement-based screening call, a role-specific assessment,[structured interviews](https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/assessment-and-selection/other-assessment-methods/structured-interviews/) with a scorecard, and reference checks. The combination should reflect the role's seniority, the risk of a wrong hire, and available time. For high-volume roles, the combination differs, but the principle holds: more evidence leads to better decisions.


### What metrics show whether your screening process is actually improving?


Track whether your methods work: Time-to-screen measures how fast your process moves and how competitive you are for candidates considering multiple offers. Screen-to-interview conversion shows whether your filters are calibrated correctly. Quality of hire at three, six, and twelve months reveals whether your chosen signals predict actual job performance.


#### Why is early turnover the most underweighted metric to watch?


Early turnover is the most underweighted metric. Strong candidates leaving within their first year signals a mismatch between the role's description and its actual requirements, a problem that traces back to vague definitions of top talent at the outset.


#### How does complexity increase when screening across different labor markets?


Using these methods consistently within one market is difficult. Using them across different job markets, qualification frameworks, and workforce cultures is considerably harder.

## How to Identify Top Talent When Hiring Across MENA


**Growing your hiring across MENA** means keeping **standards consistent** , even when things differ dramatically in each place. The way you **measure qualifications** and **plan career paths** can vary a lot across the region.


> "A candidate who has worked for **eight years** across **multiple markets** might have *far* more skills than someone whose career path is more straightforward — yet **standard screening processes** usually don't pick up on this."


💡 **Tip:** When evaluating **multi-market candidates** , look beyond the resume structure. **Cross-regional experience** strongly signals adaptability, negotiation skill, and **cultural intelligence** — all *critical* assets in MENA hiring.


⚠️ **Warning:** Relying on **standard screening processes** alone is one of the *most common* mistakes hiring teams make across MENA. A **non-linear career path** is *not* a red flag — it's often a **competitive advantage** that traditional filters will cause you to miss.


### Candidate Profile


#### 8+ years across multiple MENA markets


- **What Standard Screening Sees:** Inconsistent or non-linear path
- **What You Should See:** Deep cross-cultural adaptability


#### Single-market, straightforward career


- **What Standard Screening Sees:** Clean, easy-to-read progression
- **What You Should See:** Potentially limited regional exposure


#### Mixed public/private sector background


- **What Standard Screening Sees:** Unclear industry focus
- **What You Should See:** Broad stakeholder management skills


🎯 **Key Point:** **Consistent hiring standards** don't mean *identical* evaluation criteria — they mean applying the *same level* of **strategic thinking** to every candidate, regardless of how their career path looks on paper.


### What makes cross-market assessment harder than it looks


Job titles mean different things across MENA markets. When a role means one thing in Riyadh and something different in Dubai, recruiters default to the easiest-to-understand candidate rather than the most capable one, a consistent source of poor hiring decisions.


#### Why does misreading a hire cost more in high-mobility markets?


According to[People Connect Global's Complete Guide to HR Trends](https://peopleconnectglobal.com/a-complete-guide-to-hr-trends-in-mena-2025-expert/) in MENA 2025, 44% of employees across MENA plan to change jobs within the year. In a high-turnover market, the cost of a bad hire compounds quickly. Retention begins at recruitment, not after onboarding.


#### What happens when each country runs its own screening framework?


Most teams build separate screening processes for each country, each with its own criteria and informal standards. A strong candidate assessed under one framework gets compared against someone assessed under a different one, leaving recruiters without a shared baseline. Our[Cercli platform](https://www.cercli.com/) brings hiring, workforce management, and compliance into a single global HR system, so candidate data flows consistently across markets instead of fragmenting across disconnected tools.


### How Emiratisation and Saudisation affect candidate evaluation


Workforce localization requirements in the UAE and Saudi Arabia shape talent acquisition strategies. Private-sector employers in the UAE with 50 or more employees must reach a 10% Emiratisation rate by the end of 2026, as set out by the[Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation](https://mohre.gov.ae/en/media-center/news/22/6/2026/mohre-30-june-final-deadline-for-achieving-private-sector-emiratisation-targets-for-the-first-half) . In Saudi Arabia, Nitaqat shapes workforce composition across the private sector. Employers need real-time visibility into their current workforce makeup to make confident hiring decisions. Identifying a strong candidate without understanding how that hire affects your localization position leaves the decision incomplete.


### Candidate data, AI tools, and where human judgment still matters


AI screening tools process large candidate pools quickly, score against defined criteria, and surface patterns human reviewers miss—particularly valuable for high-volume, multi-market hiring. However, the[UAE's Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021](https://u.ae/en/about-the-uae/digital-uae/data/data-protection-laws) and Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law impose specific requirements around candidate data processing, retention, and automated decision-making. Employers using AI tools must understand what data they process and ensure they meet consent and compliance requirements. Human oversight is both a legal and practical requirement, especially for candidates with international experience or unconventional backgrounds that automated scoring may misinterpret.


Knowing who to hire and how to bring them in are two different problems, and the gap between them is where good candidates get lost.
